speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It started as a retirement savings scheme in July 1955, when many workers in small- and medium-sized companies did not receive retirement benefits from their employers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: CPF helped them to have something for retirement.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 1968, in order to improve housing affordability, CPF usage was expanded to help members buy HDB flats.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: From 1981, CPF savings could also be used to buy private properties.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This made home ownership a reality for over 90% of Singaporean households and helped them to share in Singapore’s growth.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It also gave them an asset to rely on in retirement.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 1984, in order to meet rising healthcare needs, we created the MediSave Account.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This helped Singaporeans cope with big healthcare expenses, such as hospitalisation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As life expectancy continued to rise, so did the risk of Singaporeans outliving their savings.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Members on CPF LIFE have the assurance of a constant stream of retirement income for as long as they live.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: No other retirement system tries to help people fulfil three basic needs in retirement – housing, healthcare and day-to-day spending.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Comparisons with other systems often neglect this important fact.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There is also considerable complexity mainly because new rules have to co-exist with previous rules for earlier cohorts.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Be that as it may, CPF should continue to evolve to meet the changing needs of our people.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It will amend the CPF Act in two broad areas: first, to cater to changes in employment practices; second, to clarify and streamline the administration of the CPF Act.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With the Deputy Speaker’s permission, I will also use this opportunity to respond to Mr Chong Kee Hiong’s supplementary question earlier this afternoon and provide an update on the changes we are making to the RSS in response to feedback from members of the public.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 2017, the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) had set up a Tripartite Workgroup on self-employed persons (SEPs) to look into the concerns of SEPs and make recommendations on how to address them.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In both the Committee of Supply (COS) debates of 2018 and 2019, I gave updates on the Workgroup's recommendations and their implementation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: One recommendation was to help SEPs save for their retirement and healthcare needs through the CPF system.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, SEPs must make contributions to the MediSave Account.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Unlike regular employees, there is no requirement for them to contribute to the Ordinary and Special Accounts.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Members know how MediSave Account balances can be very helpful.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They can be used to pay for medical treatment and MediShield Life premiums, which help with hospital bills.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The converse is true: a depleted MediSave Account exposes the SEP to risks of not having the support for healthcare expenses when he or his family needs it most.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Currently, SEPs make their MediSave contributions every year based on their earnings in the previous year.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This approach of making yearly contributions for past years' earnings can be improved.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Unlike regular employees, SEPs do not have a simple process to make small regular contributions as and when they earn income.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: When the time comes to make the out-of-pocket lump-sum contribution the following year, SEPs with cash flow constraints face difficulties.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As a result, some choose to pay via a 12-month instalment plan.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Nonetheless, a significant number do not sign up for an instalment plan or have stopped paying their instalments.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The root cause of this may be that these SEPs have irregular income.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Should they wish to get back into regular employment with more steady income, we have many schemes to help them do so.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In fact, last year, more SEPs switched to regular employment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But for those who remain in self-employment, we should also find a way to help them avoid slipping further back.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is what the pilot is about – helping SEPs keep up with their MediSave contributions to strengthen their protection against health shocks.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will be for a small group of about 6,000 SEPs who provide services directly to the Government and public sector agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As a service buyer, the Government can help SEPs directly transmit their contributions to their MediSave Account and then pay the rest of the service fee to them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Take, for example, Sam, who is a 48-year-old self-employed soccer coach.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: A primary school engaged Sam to conduct a two-hour soccer clinic.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The primary school paid Sam $120 for the session, of which $20 was the expense that Sam incurred.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Effectively, his income from this session was $100.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Under the current contribution model, the school would have paid Sam the full service fee amount of $120.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Well, this is because Sam has estimated that his income from this job is around $100 after taking out the expenses.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: At the same time that it contributes the $10 to Sam’s MediSave Account, the school pays out to Sam the balance $110 for this particular assignment.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We can expect Sam to take on various jobs throughout the year, not all of them with the Ministry of Education (MOE) schools.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Supposing his net trade income in total is $30,000.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: He would have to make a MediSave contribution of $3,000.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Suppose also that $13,000 of his income came from work done for MOE.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We can see that his risk of not being able to make the contribution in full is now lower – it is $1,700 instead of $3,000.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Like regular employees, Sam can make smaller and more regular contributions to his MediSave as and when he receives a payment.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is helpful as his income may be seasonal due to, for example, less work during examination periods.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: CAYE will also help Sam grow his MediSave monies.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: By contributing earlier, he will accrue more interest on his MediSave contributions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Some SEPs are more comfortable with the current model of MediSave contributions and may prefer not to be on CAYE yet.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Such SEPs can set their CAYE contribution rate to zero.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For SEPs who have not been keeping up with their MediSave contributions, we will continue to give them time to clear their back payments.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But it is better that they make contributions through CAYE.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This will help them keep up with the current MediSave obligations and prevent their obligations from snowballing.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There is absolutely no change to the obligations of the self-employed for CPF contributions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Even after Parliament passes the amendment, the obligations are the same as before.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The only change concerns how those contributions are made.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Instead of a lump-sum payment once a year, small contributions will be made from SEPs' income each time the income is earned.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As this pilot only involves SEPs who provide services to the Government, only a fraction will be affected.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If these SEPs have, in fact, been up to date with their payments, they can also opt out of the pilot.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As part of our consultations for the Bill, we had in-depth discussions with the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) and leaders of the SEP associations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They have generally welcomed the introduction of CAYE and recognise its benefits.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, they are also concerned with some of the SEPs who are already falling behind in payments.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Specifically, Mr Ang Hin Kee and leaders from the National Instructors and Coaches Association (NICA), the Professional Photographers Association (Singapore) (PPAS) and the Singapore Association of Motion Picture Professionals (SAMPP) suggested that the Government provide some matching of the SEPs' MediSave contributions when they participate in CAYE.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I have discussed with my colleagues and we agree this is a good suggestion.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Some Members may ask if we can extend CAYE so that, like regular employees, all of Sam's contributions would have been made as and when he earned an income.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have not taken a decision on whether CAYE will be extended to include payments made to the SEPs by private sector companies or intermediaries, such as for insurance and real estate agents.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Some of the intermediaries have already indicated interest.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They can see the benefit of helping their agents make MediSave payments as and when they earn an income.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is especially if the lump-sum payment happens to be required during a lull period the next year when the agent earns less income.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, let us try out CAYE first, see how well it works and decide later if and how other SEPs can also benefit.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We, therefore, plan to amend the CPF Act to be more responsive to the evolving needs of employers and employees.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Today, employers may structure wage components that are tied to certain contractual obligations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, a sign-on bonus with a minimum service period condition.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If the employee chooses to leave before the minimum completion date is up, he is required to return the sign-on bonus to his former employer.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This practice is allowed under the Employment Act.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To restore both parties to their original positions, the employee also needs to return the CPF which his former employer paid on the sign-on bonus.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, the CPF Act does not allow the CPF Board to grant refunds for this repayable component.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Suppose Daniel receives a sign-on bonus in January on the condition that he works for one full year.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: He gets $4,000 in cash and $1,850 in his CPF, which is the contribution on the sign-on bonus.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If he so happens to leave his job in March, he has to return a total of $5,850 to his employer.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Of which, $1,850 is actually in his CPF account.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Under today's rules, Daniel will be out-of-pocket for the $1,850 as CPF Board is unable to refund this amount from Daniel’s CPF to pay back his employer.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: With Daniel’s consent, his employer may also apply directly to CPF Board for the refund.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: With the changes, regulations can be made to allow members and employers greater flexibility to accept and offer such payments, knowing they can obtain a refund of their CPF contributions if the payment has to be returned.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The second and final set of amendments provide greater clarity and efficiency in the administration of the CPF Act.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Home Protection Scheme (HPS) is a mortgage insurance scheme.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It protects CPF members and their families from the risk of losing their home if the breadwinner meets with an unforeseen event, like death.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When this happens, it understandably takes some time until the claim is paid.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The grieving family will need time to report the claim.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: CPF Board will need time to process and make the claim payment to the mortgage bank or to the Housing and Development Board (HDB) in the case of HDB loans.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Meanwhile, the interest on the mortgage loan continues to accrue.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Although we have introduced CPF LIFE, the RSS is still the main CPF retirement income scheme today.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Most members aged 65 and above today receive their retirement payouts through the RSS.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: More members will start receiving their retirement payouts through CPF LIFE from 2023 onwards, when the first cohort of mandatory CPF LIFE members reaches their payout eligibility age.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: CPF LIFE will provide them with payouts for as long as they live.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: On the other hand, RSS payouts are designed to last up to 20 years from the payout eligibility age.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This takes into account the base interest rate earned on Retirement Account savings, which is now 4%.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In 2008, the Government introduced Extra Interest and, again in 2016, the Additional Extra Interest.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This benefited all members and especially those with lower balances.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It was deliberately designed as a progressive move.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: All this extra interest earned from age 55 is used to stretch the payouts beyond the usual 20 years, up to age 95 at most, to protect members from outliving their RSS payouts.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, the base payouts would have lasted up to 20 years, but with the extra interest, they last longer, can be up to 95 for some members.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have received feedback from some members who felt that the RSS payout duration of up to age 95 was too long.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Designing payouts to last up to age 95 will cover the longevity risk of up to four in five members.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In other words, only one in five members is expected to outlive his RSS payout.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: While this approach is fundamentally sound, it does mean that for the members who had remaining balances in their Retirement Accounts when they passed on, their RSS payouts could have been slightly higher.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will change the RSS payout computation to address members’ feedback on long payout duration.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The base payout will continue to last up to 20 years.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Today, all of the Extra Interest and Additional Extra Interest that a member earns from age 55 goes towards extending his RSS payouts beyond 20 years.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Extra interest earned from age 55 until the member starts his payouts will now be used to increase his payout amount.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Extra interest earned after the member starts his payouts will continue to extend his payout duration.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Moreover, the extension will go to age 90 at most, instead of age 95.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Particularly for RSS members whose payouts were originally projected to end past age 90, these changes will increase their payout amounts.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Let us say Mr Tan is aged 65 today and starting his RSS payouts.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Based on his Retirement Account savings and the current RSS payout rules, he will receive a payout of about $470 for 30 years.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: His payout duration comprises 20 years of base payouts and an extension of 10 years from the extra interest earned on his savings.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In other words, his payouts will end when he is aged 95.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, the payouts will end at age 90.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The new RSS payout rules will continue providing longevity risk protection for up to two in three members.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In other words, the majority of members on the RSS will still receive payouts for as long as they are expected to live.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For those who prefer a longer payout duration, they have the option of joining CPF LIFE before age 80.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This will guarantee that they receive payouts for as long as they live.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Allow me to also add, for avoidance of doubt, that there is no change to the payout eligibility ages or withdrawal rules for RSS members.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If you are 65 today, you can start to get your payouts.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I would also like to be very clear that members who are currently receiving payouts will either get the same or higher payouts as a result of these changes to payout rules.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: No one will see a reduction in the payouts that they are currently receiving.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Separately, we will adjust the RSS payout computation so that when members defer their payouts, or make a top-up, they will generally see an increase in their payout amount.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: All RSS members who turn 65 from 1 July 2020 will be on the new payout rules.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As per usual practice, members will receive a letter six months before their 65th birthday.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This letter will inform them that they can choose to start their payouts from 65 if they wish.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As for older RSS members who have already chosen to start their payouts under the current rules, we will apply the new payout rules to them from 1 January 2020 if the resulting payout amount is higher than their current payout.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To communicate the change clearly to RSS members who have started their payouts, CPF Board will send a one-time letter.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Relevant RSS members who are receiving their payouts will receive this letter, which will inform them whether and how they are affected.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To conclude, the changes will see RSS payout duration last to age 90 at most.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: All RSS members who are currently receiving payouts will get either higher payouts or the same payouts.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It also clarifies the administration of the CPF Act.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Together with the changes to the RSS payout rules, we are making CPF processes more member-centric.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As Members will appreciate, we will have to continue updating the CPF system to better serve the changing needs of its members.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Supplementary questions regarding the Minister's answer to RSS will be taken at the end of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I note that there are several amendments to the CPF Act.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: However, my focus today would be the introduction or provision of the Contribute-As-You-Earn (CAYE) scheme.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The Government will transmit the MediSave contributions of the SEP to his/her MediSave account.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In this regard, it is similar to the existing CPF contribution scheme which requires employers to make monthly contributions to their employees' CPF accounts.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I also note that the CAYE scheme is presently at its infancy and, at this point, the pilot run is not applicable to the private sector.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I am glad to note that the Minister has agreed to consider some form of matching contribution for this pilot CAYE.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: While the CAYE scheme is no doubt commendable and a positive attempt by the Government to support freelance and SEPs, I have the following questions for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: First, we note that, at present, the CAYE pilot scheme will only be applicable for Government contracts and there are no plans to extend it to the private sector as of now, during this pilot phase, presumably to ensure that there are no glitches and that MediSave contributions are calculated correctly.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: My question is: are there plans to extend it to the private sector?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: If there are plans, when can we expect it would be extended to the private sector?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: And does MOM foresee any resistance from the private sector?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: If the figure of 200,000 remains the same this year, it would mean that only 6,000 out of the 200,000 SEPs, or about 3%, provide services directly to the Government.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Would the Minister be able to provide some clarification as to why only 3% of the SEPs provide services directly to the Government?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Is it because the Government generally prefers contracting with bigger and more stable companies with established reputations?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In this case, what more can be done to help SEPs remain competitive?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Or would it be due to the differences in demand and supply of the nature of the services provided by the SEPs?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Does MOM see the figure of 3% as worrying?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In which case, what more can be done?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We need to ensure that these freelancers do not lose their rice bowls, amidst the economic uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: What other ways are there which the Government is utilising or considering to support the healthcare and retirement needs of freelancers in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Third, we observe that there is increasing fluidity in Singapore's employment landscape.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: For instance, some freelancers have opted to diversify their careers by picking up regular employment and working as employees by day and freelancing at night, subject to the terms of their employment contracts.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In such a situation, those involved in regular employment by day, would already have the requisite CPF contributions through the employer's plus employee’s CPF contributions needed for the big-ticket items in life, such as housing, retirement as well as healthcare bills and so on.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In this case, would the CAYE scheme still serve its objective of ensuring that these SEPs are self-sufficient?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Are there considerations for this class of persons to be exempted from MediSave contributions in respect of their freelance work and revenue, to avoid imposing additional financial constraints upon them, especially since the Singapore economy is going through an uncertain period?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Lastly, as a general observation, the CAYE scheme was developed to plug the lacuna in the law and assist SEPs with saving monies in their CPF account to tide them through rainy days and fund big ticket items.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Perhaps, in due course, it may be time to examine our laws to determine if certain classes of freelancers should be accorded "employee" status and the associated benefits, especially where their contract for service resembles an employment contract.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Perhaps, a good starting point would be to allow freelancers to be covered within the scope of the Trade Unions Act.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Both of them shared a similar story with me, about the need to use hand sanitisers regularly.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, I was curious as to why they said that.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And it is so coincidental that both asked me the same thing.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I guess the reason they gave me was that, as a freelancer, you have to look after your health and make sure you do not fall sick.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Other than the fact that you may have to pay medical bills, recuperate at home, but you also may miss out on fulfilling your clients' obligations that you promise to deliver.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That is about taking personal ownership – looking after one's health, buying appropriate insurance, topping up your MediSave account and exercising regularly.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In fact, over the last few years, Mr Deputy Speaker, I have met with many freelancers – sports coaches, tutors, actors, moviemakers, band instructors, those who do rigging in stages and outdoor events, emcees, photographers, beauticians, choir instructors, orchestra directors, fitness instructors, translators, taxi and private hire drivers, getai performers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is just to illustrate the wide spectrum of industries and vocations that many of our freelancers today come from.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is no longer the traditional tutors and taxi drivers alone.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many of them shared with me that they do adopt a healthy lifestyle and exercise regularly, contribute to their MediSave account.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some even bought prolonged medical leave insurance to cover potential loss of income should they fall sick or recover from some major surgery.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And this is especially so among younger job entrants who just became freelancers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I spoke to many of them and they shared that they think that this is only a transition job; it is not something that they will hold on to for a long time.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Making MediSave contributions are not at the top of their mind among these young freelancers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In fact, in my engagement with CPF Board, I also learnt that many experienced freelancers are also not prompt in making MediSave contributions even though there are instalment plans made available with CPF Board.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And the Minister had earlier also alluded to the same facts.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The reasons may be varied, Mr Deputy Speaker, but the outcome is the same.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Freelancers run the risks of inadequate medical provisions.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, what are we to do about this?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How do we help to place them under the safety net that every other employed worker is provided for?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Make the necessary provisions." Others ask for more Government interventions.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With this amendment, I think the role that the Government is taking on is clear.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have three requests for the Government's consideration, of which, the Minister has already answered one.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, I hope that the Government can be more proactive in supporting freelancers beyond CAYE.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The emerging gig economy is something that we are all aware of and it has created a new form of employment among many workers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One key concern is that there may be risks that may be passed on from companies to these gig workers who actually are unable to take on much risks, such as instability in their wages and not being prepared for retirement.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My hon colleague Mr Patrick Tay also alluded to the fact that food delivery drivers may fall into this category of workers who may be unaware of the risks.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For instance, I have also mentioned in my previous speeches that we, too, see many freelancers doing food delivery.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although they wear the attire of the platform provider and comply with rules quite similar to that of an employee, they are being classified as freelancers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I know that the Ministry has a WorkRight programme to ensure that those misclassified workers will be put right and be clocked back as far as CPF and other statutory rights are being provided for.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, do we need to, therefore, relook whether there is a need to re-categorise the different types of freelancers, identify those who are more vulnerable, and ascertain to see if they need to be provided and protected by the law?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, this announcement by MOM will definitely help freelancers transit to this new arrangement and I look forward to the details of the support.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This should address the training needs of not just freelancers who transact with Government buyers, but more importantly, the employability of all freelancers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I mentioned earlier some young freelancers shared that they started off freelancing, thinking it is a transition job but there are other older freelancers who also thought that it was a transitional job but, over time, it became their only full-time choice.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is because even if some struggle to improve their wage prospects or income doing freelance work, they do not possess the adequate skills to move to other jobs.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is to ensure we roll out timely interventions before the employability gap grows larger.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such new solutions are needed even as we address the unintended consequences of this new form of employment.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will ensure that freelancers do not unnecessarily struggle with employment or employability options.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This scheme actually does not make any material change to the workers' position since they already have to make a contribution to their MediSave account based on their previous year's tax returns.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What it does is to smooth out the contributions so that workers will not face a situation where they have to fork out a lump sum annually and may not have enough cash on hand to do so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This scheme is also limited in that it is to be piloted by the Government and affecting only SEPs on contracts for service with the Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A critic could give a cynical shrug to this limited move by the Government and argue that this does not change the status quo, except to secure contributions to MediSave.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am not going to see it this way.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Rather, I choose to see the CAYE scheme as a wedge that could open the door for the Government to regulate the self-employed work sector and do more for SEPs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the spirit of the CAYE scheme to address income protection, retirement adequacy and contracting issues faced by SEPs, I will speak on these three areas accordingly, in terms of the next steps the Government can take to do more for SEPs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first area where the Government can do more for SEPs is to address income protection linked to work-related injuries and medical exigencies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is despite the fact that SEPs are exposed to the same work-related injury risks as their counterparts who are considered "employees".

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With regard to work-related injuries, this difference between an SEP and an employee is more a legal artefact rather than a distinction grounded in reality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister had said in July in reply to a question on work injury insurance for food delivery riders by the hon Member Mr Desmond Choo that the distinction between employees and SEPs is that a company has control over the work arrangements of employees but has no full control over the work arrangements of SEPs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Surely, this is overstating the case in reality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the one hand, companies often have considerable control over the work arrangements of SEPs, especially for companies operating in the gig economy using membership tiering, incentives and penalties to regulate workers' discretion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the other hand, companies do not often have full control over the work arrangements of employees, especially for companies operating in the gig economy, as the same digital platforms will be used for different categories of workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe the Ministry is aware that the distinction is not black and white.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thus, Minister Josephine Teo said that the Workplace Safety and Health Council (WSHC) has been encouraging food delivery companies to buy personal accident insurance for all their riders and that major operators Deliveroo and GrabFood already do so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Given this blurred distinction between SEPs and employees in the new economy, would it not make more sense for the law, for WICA, to change to include SEPs?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, almost two years have lapsed since this initiative was started and the low participation of SEPs may be a concern.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Ministry promoted the insurance to two occupational groups that together comprised 30% of all SEPs, namely, sports coaches and instructors and taxi and private hire drivers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Also, Minister Josephine Teo mentioned in the COS debate in March this year that Grab and Gojek were providing free Prolonged Medical Leave insurance to regular drivers and that ComfortDelgro was considering.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is ComfortDelgro now providing the insurance to its taxi drivers?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would the Minister consider legislating to make it compulsory for service buyers in certain sectors to purchase Prolonged Medical Leave insurance for their regular SEPs?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many SEPs are regular contractors with the same service buyers for many years and even decades.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The SEPs in the two occupational groups fit this description.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is due to the oligopolistic or monopolistic character of the sectors they work in.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The distinction between SEPs and employees is blur in such sectors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Grab and Gojek recognise this and provide free Prolonged Medical Leave insurance to their regular drivers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It would make sense thus to legislate for income protection insurance for such sectors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second area where the Government can do more for SEPs is to address retirement adequacy, leveraging the CAYE scheme and also the SkillsFuture movement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government has urged SEPs to make voluntary contributions to their CPF if they can afford to do so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But the problem is that SEPs are already lagging in their savings compared to employees.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One way to address this issue is to leverage the CAYE scheme to encourage SEPs to make regular voluntary contributions to their CPF with the right incentive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government could incentivise this by offering a flat and thus progressive CPF top-up of, say, $300 a year to SEPs who join this programme for the whole year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Progressive service buyers could be encouraged to match the Government's CPF top-up.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As many SEPs treat their gig work as temporary jobs to transit to full-time employment, they could become disenfranchised if they are unable to tap into SkillsFuture support and resources to upskill to make the transition.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Ultimately, given the structure of our labour market and our national pension system, it makes sense to safeguard the retirement adequacy of our SEPs by helping them upskill and transit to full-time work as employees benefiting from full CPF contributions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The SkillsFuture movement cannot afford to ignore SEPs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There need to be schemes targeted at SEPs to upgrade and develop their skills.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The third area where the Government can do more for SEPs is to address contracting issues in terms of standards and the test for dependency.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is stated that the Tripartite Standard "specifies a set of fair and progressive employment practices for service contracts that all service buyers should implement at the workplace".

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The practices comprise terms of products or services to be delivered and written key terms that include names of contracting parties, parties' obligation, such as nature of services to be provided and payment due for each product or service and due date of payment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are very basic practices underpinning a contract for service.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Affected employees were paid overtime pay and CPF contributions due to them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What were the criteria used to assess misclassification?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Should these criteria be used to test whole occupational groups to see whether there is systematic misclassification due to new digital technologies allowing for platform engagement work?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In Australia, there has been discussion about the test of dependency with regard to platform engagement work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The argument is that many independent contractors signing on to work on digital platforms end up being dependent on the control and direction of the company they are working for, which looks like regular employment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Unions have pointed out that companies in the gig economy exhibit multiple features of employment, such as regulating the behaviour of workers, providing equipment to perform work, interviewing and screening workers, providing training, arranging shift rosters and so on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is the test of dependency a valid test in Singapore for distinguishing between SEPs and regular employees?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Today, SEPs are only required to contribute to MediSave.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I will cover two broad issues in my speech.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: First, the legislative history of how SEPs are treated in the CPF Act and, second, the economic reasons why this amendment is necessary, timely and should spur us to providing even greater coverage of SEPs through CPF, beyond MediSave contributions, in the future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I will start by highlighting a key change in the primary legislation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The present section 77(1)(e) provides the Minister with the discretion to require SEPs to contribute to CPF.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Clauses in section 9C, amongst others, provide the Minister with discretion in how this will be implemented.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: At first, this would appear to be a substantive policy change.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is a shift in the primary legislation from stating that SEPs may be required to contribute to CPF, to stating that SEPs must contribute to CPF.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But in fact, a reading of the legislative history of section 77(1)(e) shows that Parliament has always intended for SEPs to be covered by CPF.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Fifty-one years ago, in 1968, then Minister for Labour Mr S Rajaratnam first proposed the idea of covering SEPs through CPF.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The present section 77(1)(e) originates in the CPF (Amendment) Bill No 26/1968.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In the Second Reading debate on 1 August 1968, Mr Rajaratnam stated, and I quote, "The principal purposes of the Bill are… (iii) to enable the provisions of the Central Provident Fund Ordinance to be extended to cover persons who are self-employed and who do not at present contribute to the fund." He went on to say that the necessary regulations to effect this would be made in due course.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It appears clear Parliament intended in 1968 that CPF should compulsorily cover SEPs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Unfortunately, between 1968 and 1992 we appear to have lost the momentum to cover SEPs through CPF.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The CPF Act was then amended to provide for administering SEP MediSave contributions, including penalties for non-compliance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In the Second Reading debate on 31 July 1992, Mr Chiam See Tong asked why SEPs were asked to contribute to MediSave only, when the original purpose of CPF was to provide for old age protection in general.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Then Minister for Labour, Dr Lee Boon Yang replied, and I quote, "We are only extending this contribution to the CPF by the self-employed for MediSave at this present moment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, we would like to encourage all SEPs to contribute to the other accounts in the CPF, that is, the Ordinary Account and the Special Account.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I am very pleased that Mr Chiam supports this move.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In due course, perhaps we can take up his suggestion and move in the direction to extend the entire CPF scheme to all self-employed persons." I note that the CPF Act did not need to be amended in 1992 in order to require SEPs to contribute to MediSave.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The subsidiary legislation was enacted on 1 July 1992 under section 77(1)(e) and predates the Second Reading of the CPF Act that year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, the powers under section 77(1)(e) have always been sufficient to require SEPs to contribute to CPF.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: First, the difference in the framing of the primary legislation does matter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Section 77(1)(e) only says that SEPs may be required to contribute.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The new section 9A in this Bill says that SEPs must contribute.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In retrospect, the original discretionary framing of section 77(1)(e) may explain why we took 24 years, from 1968 to 1992, to require SEPs to contribute to MediSave.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Section 77(1)(e) does not impose any requirement to act, even though the Parliamentary intent to cover SEPs with CPF was clear in 1968.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Second, we should be cautious about framing this amendment narrowly as limited to SEP contributions to MediSave through the CAYE mechanism.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The 1992 Second Reading resulted in this narrow policy position.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But in reality, the Parliamentary intent in 1968 was for SEPs to be covered by CPF in general, and, of course, MediSave did not even exist back then.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: That is the plain reading of section 9A, with the appropriate discretion to the Government in terms of how this is to be implemented over time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I have heard the Minister’s opening speech and I acknowledge that the Government’s policy position has not changed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: SEPs are only required to contribute to MediSave.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Nonetheless, I believe we must aim for broader coverage and protection for SEPs in the goodness of time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We do not want another 24 years to pass where no progress is made on SEP CPF coverage, at least not without good reasons.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Otherwise, we might as well just limit this CPF (Amendment) Bill to MediSave contributions only, if there is no intent to eventually move towards full CPF coverage of SEPs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I will now turn to the economic reasons supporting this Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If Members look at the profile, you will find that they are generally older and less educated; slightly more than half are aged 50 and above, and 60% have less than tertiary education.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Actually, relatively few work in the so-called gig economy; most are taxi drivers, insurance and real estate agents, and other traditional self-employment vocations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The solution for them must be improving non-contributory social protection schemes, such as the Workfare Income Supplement Scheme and, of course, skills upgrading.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: My interest is in SEPs who have the earning capacity to contribute to their own social protection.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The basic reasons why SEPs should be covered by CPF are the same as that for employees.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There are behavioural biases which make it difficult for us to set aside funds for our retirement and future needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We may want to save for the future, but we face self-control problems, so spending money today always seems easier than saving money for tomorrow.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We may be loss-averse, so taking money out of our pockets and locking it away as CPF savings is psychologically difficult.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: What makes saving uniquely difficult for SEPs is that they receive income today but must pay CPF contributions tomorrow.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: CPF assessments are finalised based on the preceding year’s Net Trade Income.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This means that by the time CPF contributions are assessed and due, SEPs have long since received their income.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: They may believe that CPF contributions are an out-of-pocket loss.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Employees, by contrast, do not have this problem.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Because their CPF contributions are deducted from salaries at source, employees do not experience the same cash flow problems, or the same sense of loss, as SEPs do.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There is an additional broader economic benefit of CAYE.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Today, SEPs earn higher take-home wages than employees for doing the same kinds of work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: For example, taxi drivers may receive higher take-home incomes than bus drivers do.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is not just because of differences in the cost structure of SEPs, such as the lack of employee benefits.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The main reason is that CPF contributions reduce the take-home income of employees.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, an employee’s total wages, which includes CPF contributions, may, in fact, be higher than that of an equivalent SEP.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But it is natural for workers to make decisions based on take-home wages, since this can be spent immediately.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This wage differential between SEPs and employees in equivalent work may distort the labour market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It may explain why so many Singaporeans have found gig economy jobs attractive in recent years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It contributes to the ease with which such gig economy platforms recruit workers away from traditional employment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It may also encourage an unnecessary and inefficient shift in the labour market towards self-employment, especially if firms have a lower wage bill for SEPs because they can get away with paying less, and still pay higher take-home wages as there is no CPF contribution to deduct.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: However, there is also potential for CAYE to be applied more creatively to help our SEPs contribute to CPF and manage their finances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A common problem with SEPs is that they face highly variable incomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: For example, an external school sports coach for our schools may have to conduct training sessions continuously in the run-up to competitions but have low demand for their services during exams.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Our taxi and private hire drivers have large differences in daily earnings depending on the weather, weekends and public holidays and so on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is a problem of feast or famine.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While employees enjoy a steady income, SEPs are exposed to peaks and troughs in income.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: She might earn just enough to cover expenses on bad days.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It would not be practical or desirable to levy CAYE contributions then.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But on good days, she might earn enough profit that she would gladly contribute to CPF to save for the future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A well-designed CAYE could allow SEPs to contribute to CPF with significantly less pain than a flat contribution rate would.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This concept is built on proven research and practice.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Nobel-prize winning behavioural economist Richard Thaler, together with Shlomo Benartzi, proposed a similar programme called “Save More Tomorrow” that asks people to commit to saving more out of future income, rather than present income.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In a paper published in the Journal of Political Economy in 2004, they found that offering the chance to save for retirement starting with future pay raises, rather than present income, substantially increased both participation in retirement savings, and savings rates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: However, the concept must be adapted to the needs of SEPs.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: It is for the hon Member Assoc Prof Daniel Goh.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: It is on a point which he made earlier.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: I just wanted to check if I heard it correctly and get some clarification from him.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: If that is correct, would the operators today be alarmed that what they did voluntarily – which we had persuaded them by saying: can you co-contribute to the MediSave of the taxi drivers; can you provide subsidies for their uniforms – would now change and they should, therefore, make them their employees and start granting them paid leave, changing the entire model from a freelance one to an employee model?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: This is because that will fundamentally change the structure of the taxi industry from one where the majority are freelancers to one where these freelancers are employees.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: I am not really talking about current taxi operators and what not, but platform companies.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: Grab and Gojek and the likes of Uber are platform operators.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: When they came onto the Singapore scene, we spent quite a lot of time to persuade them to co-contribute to the MediSave; to find ways to support them in their training; to support them for their healthcare needs although they are freelance drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: They know for a fact that they are freelancers, but these platform operators actually provided support because we persuaded them to do so and they saw the logic of doing so.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: So, is Assoc Prof Goh suggesting that these platform operators, such as Gojek and Grab, therefore, treat their drivers now as employees?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Do you want to ask him for more clarifications or are you answering his query?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: I just want to clarify his interpretation of what I called for.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: But the same platform operators, whether Grab or Gojek, also offer options whereby drivers become freelancers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: So, the same platform can, on the one hand, offer people genuine bona fide freelance arrangements, but because they were persuaded to and gladly make some contributions to the riders in order that they work with you on a long-term basis and they gladly do so, but we do not consider them as employees.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: For riders doing food delivery, that is something which I called for, indeed.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I think this is an interpretation of the term "employment" by the Courts, so we will leave it to the Courts or MOM to make a decision on it.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: If executed well, CAYE could be a welcome step in streamlining the payment contribution process to MediSave for SEPs and helping SEPs better manage their cash flow.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: This is a timely amendment and answers a key concern of SEPs, who do not have the certainty of finding consistent work and face more difficulties than the average salaried employee in saving regularly for their healthcare needs.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: To ensure that SEPs are not made worse off by the introduction of this system, we must exercise care in operationalising CAYE.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: We need to make sure that the CAYE system is understandable and easy to navigate for SEPs.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Details of the payment process and even the online interface for payments must be made simple and clear, for both SEPs and service buyers.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, the educational outreach to SEPs and service buyers must be effective, in order to make the transition as smooth as possible.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: In the pilot phase, outreach can be focused on SEPs and Government Procurement Entities (GPEs).

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: However, in future phases where more SEPs may be affected, we need to ensure that the outreach extends to SEPs and service buyers in different industries and through different channels.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Also, affected SEPs should be consulted before the launch of CAYE in each phase, to ensure that the process is understood and pre-emptively iron out any potential wrinkles that may be highlighted during the consultation.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: SEPs have widely different relationships with their clients and have different degrees of dependence on intermediaries.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Also, SEPs can be paid per task or have their payments contractually scheduled over a period of time.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: This means that CAYE may not work as well or in the same way for each group of SEPs.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: To ensure a high level of compliance, consultations should be held with as many different types of groups as possible prior to implementation.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: MOM should also consider creating a one-stop resource to provide relevant information and to allow SEPs to submit queries relating to their CAYE contributions.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Some SEPs have expressed concern about CAYE potentially increasing existing delays to payments owed to them, due to the additional logistical arrangements that need to be made by the service buyer.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that the CAYE payment process is meant to be easy and automated, so service buyers should not have to use CAYE as an excuse to delay payments.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that the pilot phase will allow companies in the private sector to voluntarily adopt the CAYE scheme.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Some SEPs who are not within the pilot phase may want to participate voluntarily as they see this system as beneficial for their MediSave needs.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: There are some notable examples of private companies which provide prolonged medical insurance for the SEPs working on their platforms.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: More can be done to encourage service buyers to provide insurance coverage for SEPs, as this promotes healthy sustainability and even growth for the industry.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Service buyers and GPEs should be encouraged to factor in such costs, to minimise undercutting and provide a more level playing field for SEPs.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: To conclude, Sir, I hope CAYE is mobilised effectively to make the transition painless and help every SEP better save for their own and family members’ healthcare needs.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: While the principle of personal responsibility remains key for SEPs who have chosen this path, we can and should strengthen our support for SEPs, to help make self-employment sustainable and to celebrate the contributions of this diverse and dynamic group of workers in the Singapore economy.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: We will continue to advocate for the institutional support for SEPs because every worker matters.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many shared that their top worry is whether they can find enough work and having income stability.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Would they be given assistance, particularly those who have payment arrears?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Thirdly, would there be incentives provided to encourage this group to make their MediSave contribution?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On the CPF RSS, could MOM share the reasons why it could not give members the option of choosing the CPF payout duration?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Are there members who wish to shorten their CPF payout duration in order to receive a higher monthly payout to pay for their daily expenditure?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, notwithstanding my queries and suggestions, I support all the amendments to the CPF Act and the update to the CPF RSS.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This number is not large but, with increasing digitalisation of the economy and the technological disruptions, employment practices are changing and this trend could shift.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Tripartite Workgroup's (TWG's) Recommendation on SEPs cited autonomy as the reason that "some 80%" of SEPs in Singapore have chosen self-employment over being a regular employee.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The attractiveness of being your own boss and reaping the rewards when you succeed does come with a set of challenges and, while there are other challenges like business risks and all that that SEPs face together with the regularity of income, the focus of today's Bill is on the healthcare and savings for retirement.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Clause 5 of the Bill seeks to amend the Act to provide for the CAYE scheme.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will allow for certain persons called "collectors" making revenue payment to SEPs to be required to make contributions to the CPF funds of SEPs as outlined in the new section 9B.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While I am supportive of the amendment, I do have some comments and clarifications with regard to the CAYE scheme.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will help this group of SEPs providing direct services to the Government or public sector make smaller and regular contributions to their MediSave, and, as such, when these payments are made when the SEP receives payment for his or her services.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will minimise the risk of the SEPs not being able to make lump-sum contributions on an annual basis.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, for the contributions made, there will also be more MediSave Account interest earned.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There is, however, a very short time for SEPs providing services to the Government or the public sector to plan for this change as January 2020 is less than two months away.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Some SEPs may face transitional cash flow impact.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Will there be any assistance provided to SEPs if required and how?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Minister did say that those who have kept up with their MediSave contributions or the installment plans for their MediSave contributions will be given the option to opt out of the Pilot and I assume, if they wanted to, to start later.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But for those who do have difficulties, what help would be provided?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For the SEPs who are facing financial difficulties and are unable to make contributions for the outstanding amounts to their MediSave, the Minister did mention that some help will be given for those who are behind in their contributions to catch up.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Can the Minister elaborate what help this would be because they will not be given the option to opt out?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Feedback received from SEPs during the Tripartite Workgroup public consultation identified lack of CPF savings for healthcare and retirement needs as one of the common challenges faced by SEPs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The CAYE scheme, I believe, is a practical way to support SEPs address this challenge.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, if the CAYE Pilot scheme does prove effective in supporting SEPs make regular MediSave contributions, when will the scheme be extended to the private sector?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I also want to thank Assoc Prof Walter Theseira, in particular, for his extensive research that allowed him to share a very interesting piece of legislative history concerning intent for SEPs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I must say that Members' enthusiastic comments are going to make my response a little longer than I originally expected.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Some comments, of course, perhaps, are not directly related to this Bill.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I invite Members to file Parliamentary Questions so we can address them properly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: One of Assoc Prof Daniel Goh's questions was recently addressed by my colleague, Minister of State Zaqy Mohamad, during the debate on WICA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I believe the Member did not speak on the Act but he had quite a lot of questions there and they have also been addressed, so I shall not repeat them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We continue to work on addressing other common challenges faced by SEPs, as identified by the Tripartite Workgroup on SEPs in 2018.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Member Mr Arasu Duraisamy raised the point on payment delays.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These and other payment-related disputes can happen because of unclear contract terms.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We also introduced a template on the key terms of engagement to shape contracting norms.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh seemed to dismiss the number of companies that have already signed on to this standard.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I would humbly remind him that, actually, sometimes the buyers of services of SEPs are individuals like you and me, such as the plumber that comes to the home, someone who does an odd job.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If we think about it, actually, it would be quite unrealistic to expect individual service buyers to sign on to the Tripartite Standard.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The fact that already so many service buyers have come on board is not a small step that has been accomplished.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Of course, we will continue to build on it.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But I hope the Member will not dismiss it too lightly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There is a lot of effort involved, and if he would like to get involved with promoting it, we welcome it, too.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In addition, we have supported the development of skills training, both technical and non-technical, for SEPs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Relevant Skills Framework that SkillsFuture Singapore puts out now takes into account the needs of SEPs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Keep in mind that this product is relatively new to the market.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, 30,000 is really not a bad start.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is already about half of those in occupations like private hire car drivers and taxi drivers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As to whether the take-up can increase, certainly, we will be keen to promote it.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But we have to leave it to the SEPs to decide for themselves whether and to what degree self-employment is their main source of income, for which PML protection is important.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Keep in mind that quite a lot of them have other sources of income.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Also, for some of the SEPs, it will always be the case that they assess that their risks are very low and they would rather not have to incur the upfront costs of PML.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The pilot allows us to try out this new system among a small group of about 6,000 SEPs, gather feedback from users and iron out any glitches, as Mr Ang Hin Kee pointed out.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Patrick Tay, Ms Jessica Tan and Mr Zainal Sapari asked if CAYE could be extended to the private sector.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Arasu Duraisamy asked if they can volunteer instead.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We can decide later, depending on the results of the pilot.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But those who wish to volunteer are welcome to approach us to explore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Similarly, we can consider Mr Patrick Tay's suggestion to explore extending the scope of the Trade Unions Act to SEPs if supported by the associations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira is in favour of extending compulsory CPF contributions to Ordinary and Special Account savings.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But he also said in the goodness of time, but not 24 years.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As I was listening to him, Assoc Prof Daniel Goh's expression of concerns about SEPs' retirement adequacy came to mind, and I wondered if he or the Workers' Party has a view on Assoc Prof Walter Theseira's suggestion.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Does the Member also feel that in order to boost retirement adequacy for SEPs, he would support and would call for the extension of their contribution obligations to the Ordinary as well as the Special Account?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It would be interesting to hear from the Member, since he expressed a concern about SEPs' retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I should say that, currently, the Government has no plans to extend CPF contribution obligations for SEPs to the Ordinary and Special Account.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, we will continue to encourage voluntary CPF contributions from SEPs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh's suggestion on incentives to boost retirement savings is really not new.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is something we have been studying and I hope to be able to give Members an answer in the goodness of time.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Jessica Tan, Mr Zainal Sapari, Mr Ang Hin Kee, the Labour Movement and leaders of the SEP associations suggested providing support for SEPs when they participate in CAYE.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As I had said earlier, the Government is studying their suggestions seriously and will provide more details when ready.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If any one of them needs additional support, we are prepared to help based on the specific circumstances.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We can, for example, look at their instalment plan and see whether there is room to stretch it out.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Patrick Tay, Assoc Prof Daniel Goh and Mr Ang Hin Kee raised the question of whether SEPs can be reclassified as employees, if I heard the Members correctly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The difference is Contract of Service or Contract for Service.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Some of the factors used by our Courts include the degree of control exerted by the company and its ability to decide on the hours of work.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think the concept is not very different from dependency.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: MOM has applied this approach to determine the classification of work arrangements.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, MOM reviewed the contract arrangement of online matching platforms, such as food delivery riders from Deliveroo or FoodPanda.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Based on the factors spelt out by the Courts, the workers were assessed to be self-employed.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But as Mr Ang Hin Kee pointed out, depending on actual work arrangements, some of these workers could be employees, too.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, the employees and the SEPs can co-exist on work that look very similar.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We really need to drill down into the specific work arrangements and we are committed to doing so.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In cases where employees have been misclassified as "Self-Employed Persons", please be assured that we will take the employers to task.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Based on our investigations, the driver was in effect an employee because his employment terms indicated an employer-employee relationship in terms of the amount of control that the company exerted.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The company was asked to rectify and pay back the worker what he was due, including CPF contributions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked about the number of SEPs who provide services to the Government.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: SEPs tend to be concentrated in certain industries which the Government does not regularly procure services from, for example, real estate agents and insurance agents.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, the 3% should not be considered alarming in any way.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Patrick Tay also asked if SEPs who are concurrently employees are still required to make CAYE contributions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
